utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Witness. My understanding is that there's something about which you want to clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do have something to clarify because I do believe that I was quite vague in answering several questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed by all means, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has to do with sketches 01 and 02, when I said that there was some sort of misunderstanding with the OTP. Could we please have the sketch -- both sketches, 1 and 2, on the screen so that I could clarify which one is which, which is the sketch of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit P3299 -- or 3300.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 3301 as well. 3301, page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Shall we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The buildings indicated in 02 were the ones that had previously been shelled by the Federation --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption. Yes, please continue, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the sketch, 02, indicates the housing residential area outside of the KP Dom Butmir which had been shelled in the days prior to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I kindly ask you to show both pages of the sketch 01.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, you can help us. What we should upload, both pages of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The only thing I can think of is the unannotated versions of 3301, so that would be pages 1 and 3 of 3301.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the first page of 3300 is almost identical to page 1 of 3301 so we can show both pages?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, can you proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I. The sketch 01 indicates two-thirds of the KP Dom which had previously been a penitentiary of a semi-open type, has a fence around it which was some metre or 120 centimetres tall, whereas on the other side there was no protective fencing. It had either been removed before my arrival there or it never existed at all. The compound was easily accessible from that side and it was specifically that side of the compound that was mostly used after the shelling that I referred to. And that's all that I had to give by way of comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to make a comment on the military police unit we discussed. It used military vehicles which bore the insignia of the military police. I'd also like to say the following. When I said that it was the first time that I was looking at the official document containing a list of policemen and materiel and technical equipment, there was an interruption in my evidence simply because I was surprised positively and I was quite emotional looking at a document that I had last seen in August of 1992 again. It was a document that had disappeared along with some other official notes I made after my departure from that work-place. However, the Defence team asked me to look at the signature and confirm it. I wanted to make this comment because I didn't want to leave any impressions that would defeat the purpose of my being here. Over the past couple of days I reviewed the transcript of my interview with investigators a couple of times. I found the translation somewhat peculiar; in other words, I did not find it to be faithful to what I had to say and to the formulations I used. Quite the contrary, there were a couple of points which remained pretty incomprehensible as they stand in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. We'll leave it at that. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to all those in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If the Defence had more time at its disposal, it would very much like to clear up these points that remain unclarified due to various issues including translation, et cetera, but we don't have time for that. Last Thursday we left off discussing the issue of war crimes. You confirmed to us that the police force was vastly understaffed. Would you also agree with me that there was also a shortage of judicial personnel and that it took us more than a year to put together a proper judiciary?

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can confirm that in the area of my station there was no civilian court of law which would have jurisdiction for either misdemeanour or criminal cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us look at P1096 briefly, please. Do you agree that even nowadays domestic courts are seized of certain reports that were filed back in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 3 in English and 5 in Serbian. Perhaps the participants to the proceedings won't be quite clear on what we are clear on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So do you agree that still today certain Serbs, perpetrators of crimes, are being tried based on the documentation that had been gathered by the police force back in that period of time that had not been suppressed or in any way covered up by the police?

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us look at paragraph 2. This is a brief on certain aspects of the past work and the date is the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the date. Can, please, the speakers make a pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please slow down and could you repeat the number or date.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 1, the date is the 17th of July, 1992. I just want the witness to identify the document. It's already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ministry of the Interior, report on certain aspects of work done to date and the tasks ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have page 5 in Serbian and 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2: "The priority of the crime service is the uncovering of war crimes complete with all the documentation, forensic documentation, medical documentation ..." et cetera. Document any and all cases of war crimes were committed by the Serbs. Is that a position as it existed at the time by ministry?

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The institution you worked for was some 400 to 500 or 600 metres away from the confrontation line and the separation line?

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Along the stretch from your institution to the barracks, was this an area where snipers, mortars, and other artillery pieces were active? Was it a safe stretch of the road or a very dangerous one?

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The stretch of the road between the two locations you mention was definitely a dangerous one. At some periods we would even place screens 4 or 5 metres high in order to make it possible for pedestrians to move along freely. Sniper fire was a daily occurrence. Civilians were wounded or killed. What's more, in this material, I mean my interview, you can read that my own vehicle had come under fire and was hit in the front right-hand door.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Snipers were able to fire from Mojmilo, whereas mortars and artillery both from Mojmilo, Igman, and from the town itself, direct fire was possible from the town itself, was it not?

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do agree. In the main heavy artillery pieces were positioned at Igman, somewhat fewer pieces at Mojmilo, where there was a sniper and a Browning active daily. Frequently such fire could also be seen from Dobrinja. Our offices were on the second floor and the buildings in Dobrinja generally were five storeys high plus the attic. So there was daily sniper fire. And in this report of mine, you were able to see that in the office where we had our desks we came under sniper fire on two or three occasions. There is evidence to that effect in the rooms such as damage to the walls and the door to the office. For that reason we would hang blankets on the window-panes frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On pages 22 and 23 of this statement of yours you say that policeman Dragan Kablar was killed and Milovan Knezevic was wounded by sniper fire. Do you recall that as a result of sniper fire, chief of the security services centre Zoran Cvijetic was killed. I'm sorry, the relevant page is 20 and the lines 22 and 23.

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The late Drago Kablar and Knezevic came under artillery fire. It was a shell fired by the BH army, or rather, by the BH Federation. I also know that the chief of the Sarajevo centre, late Zoran Cvijetic, was killed by sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your institution, including the KP Dom and the entire compound, were within range and were frequently fired at, as the sketch indicated. Were there any more deaths as a result of shelling in addition to the two policemen we mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then Mr. Tepavcevic resorted to evacuation or withdrawal of personnel and inmates as far as Pale and Sokolac at times; is that right? In other words, from what was practically the front line they were moving deeper behind and you do mention this at page 16, lines 1 through 16.

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What lends support to what you say are the instructions sent by Mr. Tepavcevic to the Ministry of the Interior and Minister of Justice Mandic are asking for appropriate locations to be pin-point at Sokolac and Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- I think there should be a redaction of lines 5 to 10 on page 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What we have here was a document of General Galic's. In it he asks the civilian authorities to take care of civilians from the combat areas, to take care of them elsewhere, actually, because they're sending them to him in the barracks. And he doesn't mind protecting them, but they are in his way, they're an impediment there. Do you know about these civilians from combat areas, not only from Dobrinja and Kotorac, but also from places further away? Do you know that they were brought into the correctional facility KP Dom and the barracks?

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask you about paramilitaries. You pointed that out to us and this is what I want to ask you. Do you know that volunteers were regulated by the Law on National Defence and reinforced by the decision of the Presidency of the SFRY just before the break-up of the country, when -- when -- when there was a decline in the call-up, or rather, the response of conscripts of Muslim and Croat ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that all of those who came or actually the majority of those who came had reported as volunteers, whereas some remained volunteers with all their obligations towards the military and the police, whereas others turned into renegades abruptly or gradually and turned into fighters on their own? Actually, to put it more precisely. If somebody reports or volunteers and behaves in accordance with regulations for a while, there is no guarantee that at a certain point in time he's not going to avoid the front line as such and go back to urban areas and behave in accordance with his own wishes and motives?

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that. I know of cases like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned this Oljaca and his men. Did they start as volunteers and end up as paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. I want to have a clear conscience. I really cannot say. I know them as a paramilitary formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that Oljaca arrested many persons and brought them to prison, he would arrest Serbs too, not only his own soldiers, but quite simply he arrested all of those who should be arrested in his assessment?

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This statement is correct. In my documentation there were official notes that had been written by policemen. Unfortunately, this documentation is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That episode with two persons, two men, in unusual uniforms who wanted the police station to be subordinated to them in the KP Dom and to have everything placed under their command, is this really one of the absurdities of a civil war? Was that as you had described it and how did they end up? Is it true that Tepavcevic sent them to Kovac and Kovac kicked them out of the zone?

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement I gave to the investigators is correct --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The witness has already answered. It was just that there were five different questions in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was Kula considered a collection centre where interviews were conducted and through which detainees passed in order to be sent further on? Some would be released and others would be part of further proceedings? In other words, was this a type of investigation centre? Were interviews, investigations, carried out there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a collection centre where investigations were carried out and from where these persons were sent to other locations depending on the assessment of those who conducted interviews with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was of crucial importance for the fate of a given person as to whether he would be released or whether he would be processed further -- actually, was it only important what he had done or what his origin was?

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the mode of conducting interviews. However, my conclusion can be that they were sent to barracks or police stations in order to have the police force manned. You can put it that way. I think that what was of crucial importance was the location that they had come from and whether any fire-arms had been found on them or whether they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So it was what they did that was of crucial importance, not their origin?

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that is one of the criteria.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask that we take a look at 1 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is an investigation that the Defence carried out in connection with that and it shows that there had been paramilitaries, that there were persons who had been drugged, who would come to the gate, who'd pester people, there wasn't any special security at the gate, and there was basically no fence, and if there was a fence it could be jumped over, and that it was a true art to try to mollify these people and neutralise them. Was that your experience too? That, yes, hoodlums, if I could put it that way, could show up and maltreat people and officials had problems with neutralising such persons.

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, there were situations like that and how. There were persons who had lost their nearest and dearest and, as they were totally distraught, they would come and even use fire-arms. In their view, they wanted the police to act, they wanted to carry out revenge, and that's what they did. People were under the influence too. You know what? It's a war. There is a euphoria and it's hard to express this in words but there were situations like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now back in open session. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The main communication centre had its headquarters in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was under the control of the Federation forces. I think that there were only about ten days involved, not more than that. Certain attempts were made via radio; however, as you read these reports, you can see that very soon, due to a lack of professionalism on the part of persons who were operating it, it did not function.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now if we look at the communications problems and then orders issued orally. In addition to all of that, was there the possibility of abuse, that is to say taking advantage of somebody's name? If somebody would say I was with such and such a person, such and such a person told me I could do this and that, was that made possible due to that lack of communication? More specifically, could you always check whether people were telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such cases of abuse, especially when it comes to names of high-ranking politicians and officials of the Ministry of the Interior in order for something to be implemented, which otherwise would have been impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that one of the main reasons for Mr. Zuban to establish the internal inspections, the internal audit in the MUP? So all of these factors probably affected it, verbal orders, the possibility of misusing other people's names and authority, lack of proper communications system, and so on. Was all of that the reason for establishing the system of internal audit of public security stations and various other levels of police?

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this was one of the reasons. However, the Law on Internal Affairs in the then-Republika Srpska mandated the establishment of normal conditions for proper work of the Ministry of the Interior. Inspection and audit is one of the important elements of the work in the ministry because the ministry was answerable to the political leadership of the country. It had to inform them on all relevant security issues and developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement page 42 -- or actually, page 37 in English most probably. You say that it was difficult to identify perpetrators of crime, of wrong-doing, that the police force was successful in that on occasion, but that in general there were difficulties in work due to this. Can we now look at what it is that you mention was part of policing work, armed activities --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, but I just can't find where this was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I couldn't either.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 42, lines 11 through 17 in the English version; and page 37, 14 through 20, in Serbian. [In English] "... this is why the identification of all perpetrators of evil deeds was very difficult. It was difficult to say whether something was done by the military or police organisation was poor."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your view that the difficulties in identifying these perpetrators persisted perhaps throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of the basic problems in identification. At times, a perpetrator of misdemeanour or crime did not have identity papers on him which would indicate who he was. Since there was general chaos, it was very hard to intervene in any way. Even under normal circumstances, a criminal, a person who puts up resistance -- well, at times it calls for the engagement of special police units. The situation is even worse in times of war. Policemen manning check-points were unable to identify individuals even where these had identification papers on them because they were -- wore camouflage colours, had their faces blackened, et cetera. And very often, such groups of criminals moved in large numbers. At times they even had military combat assets at their disposal, such as the Pragas, APCs, and similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And their level of equipment was better than that of the police force; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at least that we were able to see in the list of equipment that you showed here, it does lend support to what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said in the circumstances of war and chaos. We don't have that reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My last question, Witness: In cases where a perpetrator could not be identified or visually even identified, were such cases documented and were criminal reports filed against unidentified perpetrators to open up a possibility of the case being resolved at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was strict attention paid to that -- to there being a trace in the documentation, and such cases were registered against unidentified perpetrators until such time as their identity was established and proceedings could follow from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ601 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you proceed before we take a break, Ms. Edgerton, if you can finish in ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Less than that, Your Honours. Actually, I have a question just relating to one document. I think I need to move into private session for the question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague. Now you're free to go. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a -- we'll take a break for half an hour and resume at ten past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karabeg. Can you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Mirzet Karabeg.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I discussed with you that part of your evidence would be admitted in writing. I need first to deal with the formalities in relation to that submission. You testified in the Brdjanin case over four days, between the 27th and the 30th of May, 2002; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You've subsequently had an opportunity to review the audio recordings of that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You wish to clarify an answer --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And for Your Honours and the accused, this appears in the English transcript at page 6159, lines 1 and 2, and the answer relates to a question put at the bottom of 6158.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, this deals with when you were questioned about a statement regarding the surrender of weapons which the Bosnian Serbs responsible for your arrest had asked you to make along with Redzo Kurbegovic and Suad Sabic and this is at transcript 6156. And you responded at transcript 6159: "We wrote it on a piece of paper, we signed it. Somebody took it to the radio station and read it there." The clarification that you wish to make is in relation to the sentence "we signed it," is it not?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you sign this statement with Redzo and Suad which was later read on Radio Sana?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And can you confirm that with that clarification the audio recordings accurately reflect your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you were asked today about the matters you testified to in the Brdjanin case, would you provide the same information to the Trial Chamber, that is, even if you would probably not be able to formulate everything in the same words, the essence would still be the same?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, I noticed a couple of names in the English transcript which need to be corrected. Clearly when the witness was listening to the audio recordings, they're not a correction for him. There is a name and then this square bracket with the words "phonetic," and this is at transcript 6071, lines 10 and 20. There's a reference to a person called Asim Medaric and then the words "phonetic."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, this is in relation to the meeting that you attended in 1991 in Banja Luka with 17 or so presidents of the Executive Boards from the Krajina area. What is the last name of the Bosniak friend that you met there from Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Asim Egrlic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that's spelled E-g-r-l-i-c?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, L-i-c with a diacritic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And at transcript page 6082, lines 20 and 21, it states that the head of the SDK was a woman called Dobrija Sanica and then the words "phonetic." What was the name of the head of the SDK?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Dobrijevic. I can't remember the first name. I know the last name is Dobrijevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I also note in the header of the transcript, and that's from page 6065, that it incorrectly states Mirket Karabeg instead of Mirzet Karabeg. And I seek to tender the 65 ter 22133, which is the witness's Brdjanin testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3303, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And with Your Honours' leave, I'll now read a summary of the witness's evidence. Mr. Karabeg is a Bosnian Muslim born in Sanski Most. He trained as a lawyer and worked in the Famos manufacturing company in Sanski Most as chief of personnel. He was an SDA candidate during the 1990 multi-party elections. He was subsequently elected to the position of president of the Executive Board, or Committee, of the Sanski Most Municipal Assembly, holding that position from the 1st of January, 1991, until the 17th of April, 1992. He describes the election results and the make-up of the Municipal Assembly, noting that Nedjeljko Rasula, a Serb and an SDS member, became president of the Municipal Assembly. He also names other leading figures in the local SDS. From around September 1991 to May 1992, a series of explosions were directed against the property of non-Serbs in Sanski Most. The witness recalls that 42 buildings were targeted, mostly private shops, cafes, boutiques, and two houses. The witness recalls one cafe owned by a person of Serb ethnicity being targeted during the same period. The witness states that the local JNA unit in early 1992 was the 6th Krajina Brigade under the command of Colonel Branko Basara. In February 1992, the SDS, together with the SOS, tried to take over the public accounting service in Sanski Most. In early April 1992, the SDS began insisting on dividing the municipality along ethnic lines and creating a Serb -- separate Serbian municipality of Sanski Most. A first step in the process was the 11th April 1992 reorganisation of the police force with new insignia and a loyalty oath to the Serbian authorities. The SDS continued to insist on a division of the municipality and wanted the non-Serbs to move to the other side of the river. Many check-points were set up in the municipality and only non-Serbs would be stopped and searched. On the 17th of April, 1992, the SDS Serbs, SDA and HDZ representatives continued to negotiate the situation. On that date, the witness and other non-Serbs including a number of non-Serb policemen, went to the municipal building where they stayed for the next two days. On the 19th of April, Rasula gave an ultimatum to the non-Serbs in the municipal building that if they did not leave by 2200 hours and surrender all arms, they would be attacked. The witness and others in the municipal building noticed a column of about 30 vehicles belonging to the 6th Krajina Brigade approaching and managed to leave the building by a side entrance before the artillery and shell attack on the building by the Serbs. On the 20th of April, SDS -- sorry, SDA and HDZ representatives met with SDS officials and military personnel, including JNA General Momir Talic. The Muslims and Croats made several requests in relation to the security of the non-Serb population which were approved by Talic at the meeting; however, these requests were then not fulfilled. Between the 20th of April and late May 1992, the situation grew worse. The witness was arrested at his home on the 25th of May, 1992, and detained in the prison behind the Sanski Most SJB building - this is scheduled incident C.22.1 - until around the 9th of June when he was taken to the Betonirka garage where he was detained for one month until the 7th of July. This is scheduled incident C.22.2. On that date, he was moved back to the prison where he was detained for a further seven weeks. The witness describes the terrible conditions of detention including interrogations and physical violence inflicted upon him and the other detainees, including one beating where he was kicked in the head and face and as a result lost all his teeth. On one occasion he was told that the beating was done based on the order of the chief of police Mirko Vrucinic. The witness did not receive any medical care while he was detained. On the 28th of August, 1992, the witness was transferred to the Manjaca camp - this is scheduled incident C.1.2 - where he was detained for two months until the 31st of October, 1992, when he was sent to Travnik as part of an exchange. The witness describes the conditions at Manjaca and the physical violence that was taking place in the camp during the time he was there. Your Honour, that completes the summary of the witness's written evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, I now have a number of -- limited number of questions to expand on some matters in relation to your written evidence which is now before the Court. But first can I just say I've spoken with the Court deputy and asked him when we're showing you any documents or if Mr. Karadzic is going to show you any documents, that we are going to enlarge them on the screen as much as possible and you also have a magnifying glass in front of you to use. Mr. Karabeg, at transcript page 6076 and 6077 you stated that the 42 buildings belonging to non-Serbs were targeted by explosives. Who was responsible for this?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Let me tell you, we knew straight away that it was the Serb side because grenades were thrown, or rather, explosives to -- into non-Serb shops. We insisted - especially I as president of the Executive Board - that the crime service of the police that was manned by Serbs only at the time investigate the matter. The answer that we were given was we are going to resolve the matter but, unfortunately, that went on day after day, or rather, night after night when these explosives --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all the other microphones please be switched off when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one clarification -- clarifying question, Ms. Sutherland. The 65 ter number of this transcript has an A at the end of its digit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, Your Honour, I should have said A, which is only the Brdjanin transcript. The complete 65 ter number has his other transcripts from other trials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, you stated that it was the Serb side, but can you be more specific as to who was doing these acts.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, specifically these were Serb defence forces --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the second sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a group of Serbs that established this kind of formation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, the interpreter didn't hear the second sentence after you said that it was a group of Serbs -- these were Serb defence forces --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Members of the Serb defence forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And is that -- does that have an acronym SOS?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: SOS, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And do you know who made up the SOS?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, we didn't know their names at the time. For example, these defence forces were headed by Tomo Delic, who together with us participated in talks, negotiations, and let me put this very simply. He lied to us. He said we could reach agreement if there hadn't been for our extremists, but later on we found out --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, sorry, can I just stop you there. In relation to the question do you know who made up the SOS, were there any locals which were part of the SOS?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you now recall the names of those persons?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I know their nicknames, Lunja, Medeni, Tomo Delic, and there are some others whose names I can't recall now. And then there are also those whom I never knew, people who had come from the villages in Sanski Most municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At transcript page 6078 when you were testifying about the February 1992 referendum for the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, you said that a small number of Serbs told you that they had voted in it. You also said that some Serbs were subject to pressure. What sort of pressure were you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Let me tell you, up until the 6th or 7th of April, 1992, we lived in fairly harmonious circumstances in relation to the times before. There were people who supported Bosnia and Herzegovina but who said: I do not dare vote because I was told that a bomb or an explosive would be thrown on my apartment. I simply do not dare, otherwise I have nothing against it. Let me give you a specific example. When the commission was set up, commission for organising the referendum, there was a man called Miladinovic, who was a permanent member of that commission, and naturally the Executive Board nominated him into that commission and he was otherwise a judge. So I asked him whether he wanted to be on that commission and he said, "Sure, why not?"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could all other microphones be switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then the next day he called me and he told me this, "Mirzo, please scrape my name from the list of members of that commission because people found out about that and they told me that if I should remain a member of the commission, they would throw a bomb on my apartment."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown 65 ter 04988.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, you were shown a copy of this document during your Brdjanin testimony of Rasula's diary. If I can go to B/C/S page 139 and page 122 in the English, I want you to look at an entry there for the 23rd of February, 1992. It's a session of the Municipal Board of the SDS. We can see here the text says: "How to behave during the referendum. "No one may participate in any other function of the referendum (electoral committee, members of electoral boards), the manufacture of ballot papers, the distribution of ballots. "No one may give permission that the referendum be held in his house. "Do not allow ballot boxes to be set up in purely Serbian local communes. "Do not allow ballot papers to be handed over to Serbs and that potential pressure be exerted on our people. "Discreetly control the work of polling places in town and in mixed communities outside of town, and pay special attention to ... those Serbs who attempt to vote and they should be prevented in that and their names noted." Now, is this consistent with what you were told at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I now wish to turn to transcript page 6102 of your testimony. You reviewed a document dated the 3rd of April, 1992. I don't intend on calling it up. It's associated exhibit 65 ter 04996, which is a decision on the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most to become part of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, otherwise known as the ARK. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'd now like to take you -- I'd now like you to take a look at a document which predates that document and that's 65 ter 04894.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I hear from the witness again who the Rasula -- Mr. Rasula was?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, may -- can you answer the Presiding Judge's question?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: He was the president of Sanski Most municipality. That is to say, he was the head of the legislative power in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the diary which we saw a part of it, is one of the associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The associated exhibit is 20591, which was the copy that was actually shown to Mr. Karabeg during his testimony in the Brdjanin trial. And at that stage it was given the Brdjanin exhibit number of P759. In that case, we subsequently tendered a certified copy of the diary, covering a wider period, and that is what is -- and that is what is our 65 ter 04988. And that is -- that was given -- that was given the exhibit number in the Brdjanin case as P759.1. And I listed both of the exhibit numbers in our notification, first of all, as an associated exhibit and then I filed the final notification when I clarified that, in fact, the exhibit that was shown to the witness was 65 ter 20591. And so then I added 65 ter 04988 to additional exhibits to be used with the witness. I'm in your hands, Your Honour, what I -- we would seek to tender the certified copy covering the larger period of time, which goes from 1990 through to 1992, but Your Honours may want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which has 179 pages?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But Your Honours may want to have 65 ter 20591 as a reference exhibit as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any observation, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think our -- first of all, Mr. Rasula is deceased and so it's impossible now to question him about what he meant by any of these diary entries. I understand it was admitted in the Brdjanin case and to some extent you can take judicial notice of its authenticity, but our position is that -- and I also accept that portions of the diary are indispensable to understanding the witness's testimony in the Brdjanin case. But as with the Mladic diaries, we -- our position is that only those entries that are testified about by witnesses ought to be admitted. But you've rejected that and you've admitted the entire Mladic diary. And so if you are being consistent, I would imagine you would admit this diary. But our position is basically the same, that for confrontation reasons we believe that only those parts of the diary that are discussed by witnesses in court ought to be admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that the case in relation to this Mr. Rasula is different from that of Mr. Mladic. The Chamber will admit only those pages shown to the witness here or at the time of the Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. If --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, you can see 65 ter 04894 on the screen. This is a decision dated the 23rd of March, 1992, that all Serbian territories of Sanski Most municipality should become part of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. When was the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: The Serbian municipality of Sanski Most was proclaimed on the 3rd of April, 1992. It was proclaimed by the Assemblymen who were ethnic Serbs and also a large number of highly educated residents of Sanski Most. This was how they voted, they did so without us knowing about it. They adopted a decision to annex Sanski Most to the Banja Luka region. That issue was not put on the agenda of the Assembly until 6 or 7th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, can I --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: In the meantime they prepared all that --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention to page 3 of this document. And it says under the exposition that this -- the passing of such a decision was necessary because "they want to remove them from Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina unjustly and without basis ..." Who is the "they" that they're referring to in this document?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: -- because I can't see the text well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could blow up just under the exposition.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It says there that this -- this was necessary, this decision, because "they want to remove them from Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina unjustly and without basis ..." Now, do you know who the "they" is being referred to in the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we need to zoom in the first paragraph; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then we can zoom in further on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, have you read the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I can read that just now. I couldn't do it earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I do, I do. This pertains to the Serbs. They wanted to secede from Sanski Most municipality, allegedly because they were subjugated, they were in a subordinate position and they wanted to secede.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who was allegedly subjugating them? Who's the "they" that they're referring to in that document?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, "they" means the non-Serbs. It actually means Bosniaks and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And was this true?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did the non-Serb representatives of the legally elected municipal authorities want to do in relation to the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Let me tell you. I would need to explain. The authorities --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you can do it very briefly, please, Mr. Karabeg.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: We had elections in 1990. We implemented the results of the elections. The SDS received 23 votes, the SDA 22 votes, and the HDZ 4 votes, and the left 9. Since the SDS received the most votes, they could elect the person for the top position, the president of the municipality, that was Nedeljko Rasula. Since the SDA had 22 votes, then they elected me as the second person in the municipality. And then the other positions were the president of the Executive Board and the vice-president, that went to HDZ. So the SDA had four members there and the SDS had three members there, and the deputy was nominated by the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: That is to say that the authorities and the organs were established based on the results of the elections.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, I'm sorry, I -- I may have confused you a little. You mentioned a moment ago that the "they" means the non-Serbs. It actually means Bosniaks and Croats. So what -- what did the Bosniaks and Croats want to do in relation to the Serb population? If you're able to tell the Chamber, could you please do it as briefly as you can.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Let me tell you, we wanted to support what was legal. That is to say, we wanted Bosnia and Herzegovina, we wanted all to live together in Bosnia and Herzegovina, we wanted the authorities to be fully functional based on the results of the elections in 1990 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the microphones be switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't want anything else other than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. I'm going to move on now to the 17th of April. At transcript page 6106 and following, you described that on that day you and a group of individuals, including the non-Serb police officers, went to the municipal building for the reasons that -- that have already been explained there. At transcript page 6155, you stated that on the 19th of April, 1992, at 9.30 p.m., Rasula, the president of the Municipal Assembly, issued an ultimatum for everyone to get out of the building and surrender the weapons or the municipality building would be attacked. If I can ask you to look at 65 ter 05008. This is a document dated the 20th of April, 1992, a regular operations report of the 5th Corps mentioning the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, transcript page 6155?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's what I said, Your Honour, but I see that it's not that page. Hold on. 6115. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, looking at this document, 05008, it says under point 3, under "Situation on the Territory in the Zone of Responsibility," that the municipal building was set on fire. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: See here, the municipal building was not set on fire; however, bombs were thrown on it. It wasn't set on fire, but the hand-grenades were thrown on the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At transcript page 6118 and following, you mentioned a meeting that you attended on the 20th of April, that was the day after the municipal building had been attacked with hand-grenades and shells. You had a meeting with General Talic, Basara, Major Zeljaja, and representatives of the SDS, SDA, and HDZ. Do you know where Major Zeljaja was stationed?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: On that day you mean? On that day, Major Zeljaja escorted General Talic when we met exactly at 12.00 noon to discuss these events.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I intervene. The witness said the hand-grenades were thrown on the building and then the witness said "after we left the building," and "after we left the building" was not recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note that they really cannot hear the witness well unless all other microphones are switched off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, when you speak, could you come closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender those last two documents, 65 ter 04894 and 05008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, both will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits P3304 and P3305 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, the document also notes that -- 65 ter 05008, which is now P3305, talks about ethnical divisions. Is that right? Was the -- was there actual divisions on ethnic lines that were occurring in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Let me tell you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all other microphones be switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told you that up until the last Assembly session was held, the situation was quite normal. Following that, the Serbs insisted on divisions, they wanted to have their part, they had various outbursts in order to create tensions between Serb and non-Serb population. They wanted in every possible way to stir up conflict because they were the stronger side and they would win in that conflict. We always tried to avoid it. They wanted to have their own police force, they wanted to have their own organs, they wanted their own municipality. Moreover, they even wanted their own parts of certain streets. For example, some longer streets had Bosniaks living in it, Serbs, and then in another part they had Bosniaks again. They even wanted to split those streets. They tried to provoke the others in every possible way. They wanted to -- the outcome -- exactly the outcome that came about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, just a couple of follow-up questions, and you mentioned that the Serbs were stronger. In what sense did you mean that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Let me tell you. I think sometime until the 17th or 18th of March, 1992, there was a withdrawal of the 6th Krajina Brigade from Pakrac. That was the brigade that came fully equipped with full weaponry, heavy weapons, and small arms, and so on, and they took positions on all check-points in Sanski Most municipality. In early days, they wanted just to formally to see people's IDs and then some seven or eight days they started searching vehicles, people who were non-Serbs --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: -- which -- yes? And the situation remained until the end, even further after we were arrested, after the 25th of May I think. That is to say that they took the entire Sanski Most municipality. They had the power, they held everything in the municipality as compared to Muslims, Bosniaks, and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, can I ask you to look at another document, 65 ter 05025. It's a document dated the 30th of April, 1992, and it's "Conclusions of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Sanski Most." In that document under point 1, it says that negotiations and discussions conducted with extremist segment of the SDA and HDZ have ended. Who were the Serbs conducting the negotiations with? Who were the -- who were the individuals from the SDA and the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: See here, they were the leaders of the SDA and the HDZ specifically. I was one of the extremists, as they put it --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: -- the discussions were attended by the president of the HDZ party as well as the vice-president. On behalf of the SDA there was the president of the party and the president of the Deputies Club and myself as the president of the Executive Board. On behalf of the SDS there was the president of the party, the president of the municipality, and president of the SDS Deputies Club of the Sanski Most Municipal Assembly. In other words, all those who held functions in the municipality of Sanski Most attended these discussions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And did you or any of the others from the SDA and the HDZ hold extremist views?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, see here --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, are you able to answer that with a yes or a no?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did any -- or did you or anticipate of the others from the SDA and the HDZ hold extremist views?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Let me tell you, according to them, the Serb side, yes. Had I been an extremist of any sort, I would not be sitting here today --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: According to you --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: -- or anyone else --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. So according to you, did you or any others from the SDA and the HDZ hold extremist views?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the SD -- what was the SDA policy in 1992 towards other ethnic groups that lived in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time? And this -- specifically the Croats and the Serbs. And if you can very, very briefly tell the Chamber that.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Let me tell you. The policy was for an independent whole Bosnia-Herzegovina where all the peoples present in the area would live together. The same applied to our parts, Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, I want to turn now to the 25th of May, when you were arrested and taken to the SJB and detained in the prison facility behind the police station. And this is at transcript page 6139. I only want to ask you a couple of questions in relation to your detention at the SJB in prison and the Betonirka garage because your arrest and detention are covered very well, very detailed, I should say, in the Brdjanin testimony. Do you know a person called Simo Simetic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Simo Simetic with an S, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was his occupation?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I think he was a butcher.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long had you known him for in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I knew him or I had known him for ten years. When I said that he was a butcher, well, I have to in fact say that he worked in an abattoir, a place where you slaughter cattle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How often would you see him around the town?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I would see him often about the town. I wasn't in his company nor were my friends, but he did socialise mostly with the Bosniaks, Muslims. He liked to make jokes, he was joyful, and he was a decent man, not prone to any outbursts or making any sort of trouble.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you see him during your detention; and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, I did see him not just once. I saw him in garage 3 when a man was arrested as were his three sons, and he was taken to the garage. And when this man Sales got in with his two sons, they were crying. And I asked them, "What's wrong with you? You are alive? Why are you crying?" But then I heard noise, somebody shouting, "Get in, get in." And then I saw his son. Simo -- well, they were pushing him --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat what he said. He was incomprehensible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, the interpreters haven't understood your answer very well. You mentioned the name of the son and then in the transcript it says "Simo." Was Mr. Sales's son called Simo or was he called something else?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No. It was Simo Simetic. Sales was the parent --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: -- the father of the three sons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what was the name of the son who you saw getting -- being beaten?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I know that one of them is called Amir and the other one Damir, I think. I think Amir was being beaten. At any rate, it was the middle son who was being beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Does he have a son called Sulejman?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Sulejman is the father.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ah-ha.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Sulejman Sales is the father of the three sons. Amir, Damir and I don't know what the youngest one's name was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In any event you mentioned that this was happening in the garage, garage number 3. Is this Betonirka garage?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, you said that they were pushing him, Sulejman Sales's son and that was where the interpreters lost you. Can you please just very briefly tell the Trial Chamber what you saw Simo Simetic doing. And could you please be very brief.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Simo Simetic stopped in front of the entrance with Sales's son, the middle son, and he was beating him outside the garage, forcing him to enter the garage though the door to it was locked. And the little one was telling me later on that he grabbed him by his head, beating his head against the door and telling him, "Why don't you get in?" I heard it, I didn't see it, I wasn't able to. But I did see Simo Simetic pushing his bloodied son into the room whilst holding a submachine-gun in his other hand and wearing sunglasses. That's why I knew it was Simo Simetic, because I saw him there and then I heard the story from the young man later. I was unable to see what was happening outside the door, but I heard the punches.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: And it lasted for a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did he have any function at the Betonirka garage that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I think he was one of the guards, but he was standing at the gate leading to the garages there. I don't think he was guarding the garages themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: And I think he was ashamed because most of us who were held there knew him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And how often did you see him there?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Betonirka or anywhere else where you were detained.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I saw him once in Betonirka. And since I was transferred from there to the prison facility and from there to Manjaca, I wasn't able to see him later.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, I want to turn now to the 31st of October, 1992. You were on a convoy sent from the Manjaca camp to Travnik as part of an exchange; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I don't intend asking you any questions today about your detention in Manjaca because it's covered in your Brdjanin testimony. At page -- transcript page 6068 of your testimony you state that after you arrived in Travnik, you and others set up the Presidency of the Crisis Staff for Sanski Most in exile. In that position or any other, were you aware of what was happening with the non-Serb population in Sanski Most municipality other than those of you who were detained or had been detained? Were those people staying or leaving the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, see here, we set up a War Presidency for the municipality of Sanski Most with a provisional seat in Zenica. Next we moved to Travnik. It was no Crisis Staff. It was a legal body of the municipality of Sanski Most provisionally seated in Zenica first and then Travnik. As president of the War Presidency, I was there to receive every convoy carrying people for exchange from Travnik to Turbe. Every year there were four to five convoys of some five to ten buses each, and it was from these people that I learned what the situation was like in Sanski Most. And it was, I think, in the month of March of 1995 that I received the last convoy. So that was the basis of my information about the events in Sanski Most. I would learn it from those people who were being exchanged in the period between 1992 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In relation to people leaving the municipality in convoys, were you aware of any requirements that were imposed by the Serb or the SDS authorities on non-Serbs to leave the municipality around -- at that time, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Let me tell you, whoever wanted to leave their native area, they had to sign a statement that they were handing over that property. They had to pay all the outstanding fees, such as tax on land, waste disposal, water-supply, et cetera. So they had to cover all the outstanding debts and sign a statement saying that they were leaving the property to someone, giving it as -- away as a present. Whoever decided to stay had to sign a statement of loyalty to the municipality of Sanski Most or -- that is to say, Banja Luka. Whoever refused to do so received threats to the effect that their homes would be blown up, that hand-grenades would be hailed at them, which is what did happen at the time. So nobody went of their own free will, though it appeared that way. In effect, it was done under threat and duress. The goal of the Serbian side was not to have more than 10 per cent of the population in Sanski Most, that everything else should be driven out, and the same went for the Croatian -- the Croat population.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, just a follow-up question on that. How -- how do you know -- what is your source of information in relation to the goal of the Serbian side was not to have more than 10 per cent of the population in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, there were these documents of theirs. There were their documents, and what's more, Gornji Mahala and Otoka, the neighbourhoods of Sanski Most, used to have 100 per cent Muslim population. We saw a blueprint which envisaged that their homes would be destroyed and new housing development built. Some 70 per cent of the homes and buildings that used to be populated by the non-Serbs in Sanski Most --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: -- was destroyed. There were neighbourhoods --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say "we saw a blueprint," who was "we" and where did you see this?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: When I say "we," I mean -- I actually mean I, I saw these documents. As a representative of the civilian government, I was among the first to go to the municipality of Sanski Most and I held in my hands this very blueprint, according to which there would have been a new housing development in Sanski Most for the purposes of the Serb population. Another project of theirs was also --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: -- well-known --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Karabeg. When you say that you saw these documents first, you're talking about after the liberation of Sanski Most in October 1995, are you not?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I never stepped foot in Sanski Most from 22nd of August, 1992, up until 12th of October, 1995, when Sanski Most was liberated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, I have very limited time. I want to show you one more document and then ask you a couple of questions, but you mentioned that "another project of theirs was also" and then I interrupted you. Can you very, very briefly explain what you were about to say.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No. What I wanted to say was this: When they shelled Sanski Most, there were streets and neighbourhoods where there was mixed population. So they issued reports over the media that those Bosniaks who were loyal to the Serb people should hang white sheets out of their windows. This was an indication for them to be able to target these very Muslim homes with artillery that was -- with long-range artillery. So that's how they were able to target them in these mixed neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, can I ask you to look at 65 ter 05115.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, Your Honour, I tender 05025.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The document that we just saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Referring to extremists?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3306, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, this document 65 ter 05115 is dated the 2nd of July, 1992. It's a decision of the Sanski Most Crisis Staff on the criteria for the possibility of departure from the municipality. The document states that voluntary departure from Sanski Most municipality shall be allowed only under two conditions, either a statement stating voluntarily leaving on a permanent basis and that they are signing immovable property over to the Sanski Most municipality or if they exchange the property with someone else. Is this consistent with what you were aware of at the time as to the requirements for leaving the Sanski Most municipality by the non-Serb population? And I think you've alluded to it a little earlier in your answers.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we intervene in the translation. Took place at the disposal of does not mean to sign property over. It is stated here that the property should -- shall be signed over to the municipality of Sanski Most, whereas the original document reads it shall be signed over or it shall be handed over to the municipality of Sanski Most at their disposal, and that's something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, do you see the original?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Does it state what Mr. Karadzic is stating it states?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Can it be enlarged a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Actually I think it's -- I think it would be better if the interpreters read out the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or they can translate as we read. That's probably -- somebody could read out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yeah. If we could read Article 1 of the decision, please. Voluntary departure from Sanski Most municipality shall be allowed to families and persons -- or, sorry, I'm reading the English translation which -- is it possible the interpreters could read Article 1, please, of the document. It's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or, Mr. Karadzic, can you kindly read Article 1.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. "Voluntary departure from the territory of the municipality of Sanski Most is hereby permitted to the families and individuals who give a statement to the appropriate municipal body of administration (Municipal Secretariat for general administration, physical planning and housing and utilities) to permanently leave the territory of the municipality and leave their immovable property at the disposal of the municipality of Sanski Most." This is what I'm interested in -- or rather, I can finish. And I continue: "The individuals referred to in the paragraph above may take out all their movable property from the territory of the municipality where they have drawn up a list of property to be certified by the appropriate body of municipal administration." That is the end of the article.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I explain this? Mr. Karadzic, you would perhaps be right in saying "leave at the disposal of." However, do not disregard the bit where it says "the citizens who leave the municipality of Sanski Most permanently," permanently, that's what it says. This means that this citizen who permanently leaves this area will never get the property back if their departure is permanent.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Permanently, off you go, and it is well-known what the procedure is when the transfer of property is concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic just read out the article for the benefit of us understanding the article. Do you have more?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But then we can take a break or you would like to go on until the break?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have approximately three questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed then, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, the document that you see in front of us, is that consistent with what you were aware of at the time as to the requirements for leaving the Sanski Most municipality? Were people -- were people voluntarily leaving --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were people voluntarily leaving?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not a single man said that he had left voluntarily. They were crying because they had to leave. Nevertheless, they said freedom is freedom. The pressure was so great all the time, torture as well against them, and then they had to leave the municipality of Sanski Most. And all of them said to me: It seems that their plan, or rather, wish will be carried out, namely, that Sanski Most will not have more than 10 per cent Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honour, I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3307, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have two more questions, Mr. Karabeg -- three. What was the approximate figure of the non-Serb population pre-war, that is, around the 1991 census, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I do know. I took part in these censuses too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Are you able to give us the --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: This is the way it was --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- the figures, I just need the figures, please, for the non-Serb population if you're able to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Non-Serbs, there were 28.000 of them and 4.700 Croats --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not hear the other figure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, you gave two figures, one was for the Muslims and one was for the Croats; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
